title: Venus evanescit. Carthago surgens
titleEn: Venus Vanishes; Carthage Rising — Aeneid I.387–465
about: Venus, still in her huntress's disguise, tells Aeneas that his lost ships are safe, and proves it by the omen of twelve swans that an eagle scattered and that now sing, returned, in the open sky. She turns away, and her rosy neck, scented hair and trailing robe show her a goddess; Aeneas, recognising his mother, runs after her and complains that she mocks him with false shapes and will not let him clasp her hand or speak to her in her own form. She does not answer. Instead she wraps him and Achates in a thick mist so that no one can see or stop them, and goes off to her temple at Paphos. The two climb a hill above Carthage and watch the Tyrians at work: raising walls, digging harbours, laying theatre foundations, hewing columns, all as busy as bees in early summer. Aeneas, who has no city, calls them fortunate, and passes unseen among them. In the middle of the town is a grove where the Carthaginians dug up a horse's head, Juno's omen of a warlike and prosperous people, and there Dido is building a great temple to Juno. While waiting for the queen, Aeneas looks at the pictures on its walls and finds the battles of Troy, with Priam, the sons of Atreus and Achilles. He stops in tears and says to Achates that there is no place in the world untouched by their sufferings, that even here honour has its rewards, that events draw tears and that the lot of mortals stirs the mind, and bids him put away his fears, since this fame will bring them some safety. He feeds his mind on the empty painting, groaning, and his face runs wet.

sentences.t:
“Quisquis es, haud, credo, invisus caelestibus auras
vitalis carpis, Tyriam qui adveneris urbem.
sentences.l:
“Whoever you are, not, I believe, hated by the heavenly ones, the airs
of life you take, you who have come to the Tyrian city.
sentences.i: “Whoever you are, you draw the breath of life, I think, with no grudge from heaven, now that you have reached the Tyrian city.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Venus's speech (to 401). She is still the huntress of I.314 ff. and does not reveal herself. 'Quisquis es' — 'whoever you are'. 'haud, credo, invisus caelestibus' — 'not, I believe, hated by the heavenly ones': 'invisus' is here the adjective 'hated, hateful' (from 'invideo'; a different word from 'invisus' 'unseen'), with the dative 'caelestibus' (the gods; plural dative, 'to the heaven-dwellers'). 'auras vitalis carpis' — 'you pluck the vital airs', that is 'you live and breathe'; 'vitalis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is (you'll see this constantly: 'omnis', 'montis'). 'qui adveneris' — a relative clause with the perfect subjunctive that gives the reason, 'you who have arrived', so 'since you have arrived'. Her logic is courteous and sly: a man who reached Carthage alive cannot be an enemy of the gods. Homeric model: Athena, disguised as a girl, meets Odysseus near the Phaeacian city (Odyssey 7).

sentences.t:
Perge modo, atque hinc te reginae ad limina perfer,
Namque tibi reduces socios classemque relatam
nuntio, et in tutum versis aquilonibus actam,
ni frustra augurium vani docuere parentes.
sentences.l:
Go on only, and from here to the queen's thresholds carry yourself;
for to you returned comrades and the fleet brought back
I announce, and into safety, the north winds having been turned, driven,
unless in vain augury vain parents taught me.
sentences.i: Only go on, and carry yourself from here to the queen's threshold; for I tell you that your comrades are restored to you, and your fleet brought back and driven to safety as the north winds shifted, unless my parents taught me augury for nothing.
sentences.n: 'Perge modo' — 'only go on': 'modo' here is 'just', a gentle urging; the phrase returns at 401 and frames the speech. Line 390 begins with a capital after a comma in Greenough's print ('Namque'); the capital is his. 'limina' — plural of 'limen', 'thresholds', for the door of a house or palace. 'reduces socios classemque relatam… actam' — 'nuntio' takes an accusative and infinitive with 'esse' left out, 'I announce (your comrades) restored, (your fleet) brought back and driven…'; 'reduces' is an adjective agreeing with 'socios', and 'relatam' and 'actam' are perfect passive participles agreeing with 'classem'. 'versis aquilonibus' — ablative absolute, 'the north winds having been turned': the storm of I.81–123 has shifted. 'ni' = 'nisi', 'unless'. 'frustra… vani' — 'in vain… vain', the same word-stem twice: her parents would be 'vani', 'idle, unreliable', if their teaching was in vain. 'docuere' — 'docuerunt': '-ere' for '-erunt', which you will see constantly. 'docere' takes two accusatives, 'taught me augury', 'me' being understood.

sentences.i: Look at the twelve swans, rejoicing in their ranks, that Jove's eagle had been harrying from the heights across the open sky;
sentences.n: 'bis senos' — 'twice six', a distributive, 'twelve'. The numbers fit the lost ships: Aeneas set out with twenty (I.381), seven came into harbour with him (I.170), and one was seen to go down in the storm (I.113–117), which leaves twelve unaccounted for; Venus's own comparison of swans to ships follows at 397–400. 'laetantis' — Greenough's accusative plural in -is. 'Iovis ales' — 'Jove's bird', the eagle, the bird of Jupiter; here it has been harrying the swans. 'aetheria quos lapsa plaga' — 'lapsa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'labor' ('slip, glide'), 'having glided down from the airy region' (ablative of the place from which). 'aperto… caelo' stand either side of 'turbabat' (the open sky), where the eagle is the aggressor. 'turbabat' — imperfect, 'was (until now) harrying, scattering'. The omen is a Roman augury: a flight of birds read as a sign of events to come.

sentences.t:
nunc terras ordine longo
aut capere, aut captas iam despectare videntur:
sentences.l:
now the lands in long order
either to be taking, or, taken, now to look down on, they seem:
sentences.i: now, in long array, they seem either to be settling on land or, having settled, to look down upon it:
sentences.n: 'videntur' — passive of 'video', 'seem' (not 'are seen'), with the infinitives 'capere' and 'despectare'. 'terras capere' — 'take the lands', 'reach the earth, settle on it'. 'captas' agrees with 'terras', 'having been taken'. 'despectare' is the frequentative of 'despicere', 'to look down on repeatedly, survey'. 'aut… aut' — 'either… or'. 'ordine longo' — ablative of manner, 'in a long line'. The colon sets up the comparison that follows, 'ut… haud aliter' ('as… not otherwise').

sentences.t:
ut reduces illi ludunt stridentibus alis,
et coetu cinxere polum, cantusque dedere,
haud aliter puppesque tuae pubesque tuorum
aut portum tenet aut pleno subit ostia velo.
sentences.l:
as those, returned, play with their whirring wings,
and in a flock have girt the sky, and songs have given,
not otherwise both your ships and the youth of your men
either hold the harbour or with full sail enter the mouth.
sentences.i: just as those birds, safely back, sport on their whirring wings, ring the sky in a flock and give out their song, so your ships and the young men of your company are either in harbour now or entering its mouth under full sail.
sentences.n: A simile in the Latin pattern 'ut… haud aliter' ('as… not otherwise'): the swans' return to the sky is the ships' return to harbour. 'illi' — the swans ('those'). 'reduces' — an adjective with the sense 'brought back safely' (compare 390, 'reduces socios'). 'stridentibus alis' — ablative, 'with whirring wings'. 'cinxere… dedere' — '-ere' for '-erunt' again ('cinxerunt', 'dederunt'); the perfects state what the swans have already done. 'cantus dare' — 'give out songs'. 'puppesque tuae pubesque tuorum' — 'tuorum' is the ordinary genitive plural masculine of 'tuus' used as a noun, 'of your (people)'. The '-que… -que' pairing ('both… and') is the double enclitic you'll see constantly. 'tenet… subit' — the verbs are singular with a compound subject ('puppes' and 'pubes'), agreeing with the nearer, 'pubes'. 'pleno velo' — ablative of manner, 'under full sail'; 'ostia' is the mouth, the entrance of the harbour.

sentences.t: Perge modo, et, qua te ducit via, dirige gressum.”
sentences.l: Go on only, and, where the road leads you, direct your step.”
sentences.i: Only go on, and direct your steps wherever the road leads.”
sentences.n: The end of Venus's speech, marked in the edition by the closing mark after the stop. 'Perge modo' repeats 389, and so brackets her speech. 'qua' is an adverb, 'where' (the ablative feminine of the relative, 'by which way'); 'dirige' is the imperative of 'dirigo'. 'gressum' — the singular for 'steps', a collective use that you'll see again.

sentences.t:
Dixit, et avertens rosea cervice refulsit,
ambrosiaeque comae divinum vertice odorem
spiravere, pedes vestis defluxit ad imos,
et vera incessu patuit dea.
sentences.l:
She spoke, and turning away with rosy neck she shone,
and ambrosial hair from the head a divine fragrance
breathed, to the lowest feet the robe flowed down,
and true by her gait was revealed the goddess.
sentences.i: She spoke, and as she turned away her neck shone rosy; her ambrosial hair breathed a heavenly fragrance from her head, her robe slipped down to her very feet, and the way she moved showed her a true goddess.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Dixit' — an abrupt perfect, 'she said', closing the speech. 'avertens' — 'turning (herself) away'. 'rosea cervice' — ablative of respect or manner, 'with her rosy neck': the epiphany begins with the neck's light. 'ambrosiae comae' — 'ambrosial hair': 'ambrosia' is the food and perfume of the gods. 'spiravere' — '-ere' for '-erunt' (you'll see this constantly). 'vertice' — ablative of the place from which, 'from the crown of her head'. 'pedes vestis defluxit ad imos' — 'ad' governs 'pedes', set before 'vestis' with 'imos' after the verb: the robe, which at I.320 was gathered in a knot for the hunt, leaving the knee bare, flows down to her lowest feet. 'incessu' — ablative of means, 'by her gait': here the goddess is known by her walk. 'vera… dea' — 'a true goddess', predicative nominative. Compare Helen's recognition of the disguised Aphrodite in the Iliad (Book 3), by her neck, her breast and her eyes.

sentences.t:
Ille ubi matrem
adgnovit, tali fugientem est voce secutus:
sentences.l:
He, when his mother
he recognised, the one fleeing with such a voice followed:
sentences.i: When he recognised his mother, he followed her as she fled, with these words:
sentences.n: 'adgnovit' — Greenough's spelling (the familiar form is 'agnovit'); 'ubi' with the perfect means 'when, as soon as'. 'est secutus' — the perfect of the deponent 'sequor', with the auxiliary 'est' placed before the participle. 'fugientem' — present participle, 'the fleeing one', object of 'secutus'. 'voce' — 'with (his) voice': he pursues her with words, since he cannot catch her. The colon opens his speech (to 409).

sentences.t:
“Quid natum totiens, crudelis tu quoque, falsis
ludis imaginibus?
sentences.l:
“Why your son so often, you too cruel, with false
images do you mock?
sentences.i: “Why do you, too, cruel as you are, mock your son so often with false appearances?
sentences.n: The opening mark opens Aeneas's speech. 'Quid' — 'why' (an accusative of respect, 'in respect of what'). 'natum' — 'son', object of 'ludis'. 'crudelis tu quoque' — 'you too (are) cruel': 'too' because the gods, above all Juno, have been cruel to him. 'ludis' — 'mock', with the ablative 'imaginibus', the false shapes (the huntress's shape is one). 'falsis… imaginibus' frames the question around 'ludis'.

sentences.t:
Cur dextrae iungere dextram
non datur, ac veras audire et reddere voces?”
sentences.l:
Why to join right hand to right hand
is it not granted, and true voices to hear and give back?”
sentences.i: Why am I not allowed to clasp hand in hand, and to hear true words and answer them?”
sentences.n: The second question, and the end of the speech (closing mark after the question mark). 'datur' — impersonal 'it is granted', with the infinitives as subject: 'non datur… iungere… audire et reddere' — 'it is not granted to join… to hear and to return'. 'dextrae iungere dextram' — 'to join right hand to right hand' (dative of the thing joined to, and accusative object). 'veras… voces' — 'true voices': a real conversation, with her in her own shape, against the 'falsis imaginibus' of the previous unit. 'reddere' here is 'to give back, answer'.

sentences.t: Talibus incusat, gressumque ad moenia tendit:
sentences.l: With such words he reproaches, and his step toward the walls he stretches:
sentences.i: With such words he reproaches her, and presses on toward the walls of the city:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Talibus' — 'with such (words)', the noun ('verbis') understood. 'incusat' — 'accuses, reproaches'. 'gressum tendit' — 'stretches his step', 'pushes on'. The colon leads to what Venus does next, not to speech; she makes no reply to the reproach.

sentences.t:
at Venus obscuro gradientes aere saepsit,
et multo nebulae circum dea fudit amictu,
cernere ne quis eos, neu quis contingere posset,
molirive moram, aut veniendi poscere causas.
sentences.l:
but Venus with dark air enclosed the walkers,
and with a thick mantle of mist the goddess poured around them,
lest anyone be able to see them, or lest anyone to touch them,
or to contrive delay, or demand the causes of their coming.
sentences.i: But Venus wrapped the travellers in a dark veil of air, and the goddess poured a deep mantle of mist about them, so that no one should see them or touch them, or hold them back, or ask why they had come.
sentences.n: 'at' — 'but': she gives no answer. 'aere' — 'air', here thick air, 'mist' ('aer', a Greek loanword; not 'aes', 'bronze', as at 448–449): she makes them invisible. 'saepsit' — perfect of 'saepio', 'hedge in'. 'multo… amictu' — 'with a thick mantle'; 'nebulae' is genitive, 'of mist'. 'circum' is an adverb, with 'fudit'. 'ne quis… neu quis' — a purpose clause (negative): 'lest anyone… or lest anyone'. 'posset' governs all four infinitives: 'cernere', 'contingere', 'molirive' ('moliri' + '-ve', 'or') and 'poscere'. 'moram moliri' — 'to contrive a delay'. 'veniendi… causas' — gerund in the genitive, 'the causes of coming'. Homeric model: Athena pours a mist around Odysseus so that no Phaeacian will stop him and ask questions (Odyssey 7).

sentences.t:
Ipsa Paphum sublimis abit, sedesque revisit
laeta suas, ubi templum illi, centumque Sabaeo
ture calent arae, sertisque recentibus halant.
sentences.l:
Herself to Paphos on high she goes, and her abodes revisits
glad, her own, where to her a temple, and a hundred with Sabaean
incense glow altars, and with garlands fresh breathe.
sentences.i: She herself goes off on high to Paphos and, glad, revisits her own dwelling, where she has a temple and a hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense and are fragrant with fresh garlands.
sentences.n: 'Ipsa' — 'she herself', as against the two Trojans she has left. 'Paphum' — Paphos in Cyprus, the chief seat of her cult, a place-name in the accusative with no preposition ('to Paphos'). 'sublimis' — 'raised up, aloft', predicative. 'illi' — dative of possession ('templum illi', 'a temple (is) to her', that is 'she has'), with 'est' understood; the altars have their own verb, 'calent'. 'Sabaeo ture' — frankincense from Saba (Sheba, in Arabia), 'ablative of means' with 'calent'. 'sertis recentibus halant' — 'breathe with fresh garlands', a fragrance-verb used with the ablative. Homeric model: in the Odyssey's song of Ares and Aphrodite, Aphrodite goes to Paphos, where she has a precinct and a fragrant altar (Odyssey 8); here the altars number a hundred.

sentences.t: Corripuere viam interea, qua semita monstrat.
sentences.l: They snatched the way meanwhile, where the path shows.
sentences.i: Meanwhile they hurried on along the way the path showed.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Corripuere' — '-ere' for '-erunt' (you'll see this constantly); the subject (Aeneas and Achates) is not named. 'viam corripere' — 'snatch up the road', a vivid idiom, 'hurry along'. 'qua' — 'where' (compare 401). 'monstrat' — present tense, 'shows': the road is described as it lies.

sentences.t:
Iamque ascendebant collem, qui plurimus urbi
imminet, adversasque adspectat desuper arces.
sentences.l:
And now they were climbing a hill, which very large over the city
hangs, and the facing citadels looks upon from above.
sentences.i: And now they were climbing the hill that looms huge over the city and looks down on the towers facing it.
sentences.n: 'iamque' — 'and now'. 'ascendebant' — imperfect, 'were climbing', which sets the scene for what follows. 'plurimus' — 'very great, very massive', agreeing with 'qui' (the hill). 'urbi imminet' — 'hangs over the city' (dative with the compound verb). 'adversas… arces' — 'the facing citadels', the high places of the city across from the hill; 'adspectat' is the frequentative of 'aspicio' ('look upon'). 'desuper' — 'from above'.

sentences.t:
Miratur molem Aeneas, magalia quondam,
miratur portas strepitumque et strata viarum.
sentences.l:
Marvels at the mass Aeneas, huts once,
marvels at the gates and the din and the paved ways of the streets.
sentences.i: Aeneas marvels at the mighty mass, where once there were only huts, marvels at the gates, the din, and the paved streets.
sentences.n: 'Miratur… miratur' — anaphora (the same word opening both lines), which carries the wonder. 'molem' — 'mass', here 'great structure, building-works'. 'magalia' — the Punic word for 'huts', in apposition to 'molem' ('the mass, (once) huts'); 'quondam' — 'once'. The thought is that what is now a city was a settlement of huts. 'strata viarum' — 'the paved parts of the streets': 'strata' is a neuter plural participle used as a noun, with the genitive 'viarum' dependent on it. 'strepitum' — the din (of the busy city).

sentences.t:
Instant ardentes Tyrii pars ducere muros,
molirique arcem et manibus subvolvere saxa,
pars optare locum tecto et concludere sulco.
sentences.l:
Press on, burning, the Tyrians, part to draw out walls,
and to build the citadel and with hands to roll up stones,
part to choose a site for a roof and to enclose it with a furrow.
sentences.i: The Tyrians press eagerly on: some are drawing out the walls, some building the citadel and rolling up stones with their hands, and some choosing a site for a house and marking it off with a furrow.
sentences.n: 'instant' — 'press on, are busy at', with infinitives ('ducere', 'molirique', 'subvolvere', 'optare', 'concludere'; poetic for 'press on to do'). 'ardentes' — 'burning, eager', predicative. 'pars… pars' — 'part… part', in apposition to the subject 'Tyrii' (partitive apposition, a Latin habit); the construction continues in 427 as 'hic… alii'. 'ducere muros' — 'draw out walls'. 'tecto' — dative of purpose, 'for a roof, a dwelling'. 'sulco' — ablative of means: a furrow ploughed round a site was the Roman way of marking out a town's line. 'molirique' — 'moliri' + '-que'.

sentences.t: [Iura magistratusque legunt sanctumque senatum;]
sentences.l: [Laws and magistrates they choose, and a holy senate;]
sentences.i: [They choose laws, magistrates and a venerable senate;]
sentences.n: Greenough prints this line in square brackets as spurious (a line that editors suspect is not Virgil's), and it is kept here in brackets. The passage runs without it: 'pars… pars' (423–425) is followed straight by 'hic… alii' (427). 'legunt' — 'choose, elect'; 'iura magistratusque… senatum' — three objects in a list ('que… que'). 'sanctum' — 'holy, inviolable', of the senate's dignity. The three objects are Roman institutions.

sentences.t: hic portus alii effodiunt;
sentences.l: here harbours others dig out;
sentences.i: Some here dig out harbours;
sentences.n: 'hic' — 'here' (the adverb, 'at this spot'), the first of two 'hic' clauses ('here… there'); 'alii' — 'others, some', the subject; the second clause has its own 'alii' in 428. 'portus' — 'harbours', accusative plural 4th declension. 'effodiunt' — 'dig out, excavate'.

sentences.t:
hic alta theatris
fundamenta locant alii, immanisque columnas
rupibus excidunt, scaenis decora alta futuris.
sentences.l:
here deep for theatres
foundations lay others, and huge columns
from the cliffs cut out, tall adornments for stages to be.
sentences.i: Others lay deep foundations for theatres and hew huge columns from the cliffs, tall adornments for stages yet to be.
sentences.n: 'hic' — 'here'. 'alta… fundamenta' — 'deep foundations', with 'alta' placed in front of the dative 'theatris' ('for theatres'). 'locant' — 'place, lay'. 'immanis' — Greenough's accusative plural in -is, with 'columnas'. 'rupibus' — ablative, 'from the cliffs' (separation, without 'ex'). 'excidunt' — 'cut out' (from 'excido'). 'decora alta' — 'tall ornaments', neuter plural in apposition to 'columnas'. 'scaenis… futuris' — dative of purpose, with 'futuris' the future participle of 'sum' ('about to be').

sentences.t:
Qualis apes aestate nova per florea rura
exercet sub sole labor,
sentences.l:
Such as bees in the new summer through flowering fields
exercises beneath the sun toil,
sentences.i: The labour is like that which, in early summer, sets bees to work in the sun over the flowering fields,
sentences.n: A simile begins, and runs to 436. 'Qualis… labor' — 'such as… toil': the word that would answer 'qualis' ('talis', 'such') is not written, and the sense comes only at 436 ('fervet opus'). 'apes' — the object of 'exercet' ('keeps busy, sets to work'); 'labor' is the subject, held back to the end of the clause. 'aestate nova' — ablative of time, 'in the new summer'. Bees as a simile for a busy crowd are Homeric (the Achaeans gathering like bees, Iliad 2). It has to be cut at commas, because the period is seven lines long.

sentences.t:
cum gentis adultos
educunt fetus,
sentences.l:
when of the tribe the grown
they lead out offspring,
sentences.i: when they lead out the full-grown young of their race,
sentences.n: 'cum' — 'when', the first of three tasks of the hive. 'gentis adultos educunt fetus' — 'gentis' is the genitive 'of the race' and 'adultos' ('grown') with 'fetus' ('offspring', accusative plural of the fourth declension). 'educunt' — 'lead out' (the swarm's young). The cut here is at a comma, as before.

sentences.t:
aut cum liquentia mella
stipant et dulci distendunt nectare cellas,
sentences.l:
or when flowing honey
they pack and with sweet nectar swell the cells,
sentences.i: or when they pack the liquid honey and fill the cells to bursting with sweet nectar,
sentences.n: 'aut cum' — 'or when', the second task. 'liquentia' — 'liquid, flowing' (present participle of 'liqueo', used as an adjective). 'stipant' — 'pack, press together'. 'distendunt' — 'swell, stretch out', with the ablative 'dulci nectare' ('with sweet nectar'). The cells are 'cellae', the cells of the honeycomb.

sentences.t:
aut onera accipiunt venientum, aut agmine facto
ignavom fucos pecus a praesepibus arcent:
sentences.l:
or burdens they receive of those arriving, or a column having been formed
the drones, a lazy herd, from the hives drive away:
sentences.i: or take the loads of those coming in, or form a column and drive the idle herd of drones from the hives:
sentences.n: 'aut… aut' — 'or… or', the third and fourth tasks. 'venientum' — the old genitive plural for 'venientium' ('of those coming'), the '-um' form you'll see constantly. 'onera accipiunt' — 'take the loads' of the foragers. 'agmine facto' — ablative absolute, 'a column having been formed'. 'ignavom' — Greenough's spelling of 'ignavum', 'idle', agreeing with 'pecus'. 'fucos pecus' — 'the drones, a herd': 'pecus' (singular, 'herd, flock') is in apposition to 'fucos'. 'a praesepibus' — 'away from the hives' ('praesepes', enclosures).

sentences.t: fervet opus, redolentque thymo fragrantia mella.
sentences.l: seethes the work, and smell of thyme the fragrant honeys.
sentences.i: the work glows hot, and the fragrant honey smells of thyme.
sentences.n: The simile's answer: 'fervet opus' — 'the work seethes', where the 'talis' answering 'qualis' (430) would stand. 'redolent' — 'smell of', with the ablative 'thymo' ('with thyme'); 'mella' — plural for the honey, 'honeys'; 'fragrantia' agrees with it.

sentences.t: “O fortunati, quorum iam moenia surgunt!”
sentences.l: “O fortunate ones, whose now the walls are rising!”
sentences.i: “How fortunate you are, you whose walls are rising even now!”
sentences.n: Aeneas speaks (to 437 only; the narrator takes over in 438). 'O fortunati' — vocative, 'O fortunate ones'. 'quorum… moenia' — 'whose walls': the relative clause. 'iam' — 'already, now'. The words carry Aeneas's longing: he has no city yet. Compare 'O terque quaterque beati' (I.94), the earlier outcry of the same kind. Both opening and closing marks are in this unit.

sentences.t: Aeneas ait, et fastigia suspicit urbis.
sentences.l: Aeneas says, and the rooftops looks up at of the city.
sentences.i: So says Aeneas, gazing up at the roofs of the city.
sentences.n: 'ait' — 'says', put after the speech, in the Latin way. 'fastigia' — 'roofs, gables, summits'. 'suspicit' — 'looks up at', from 'suspicio' (compare the verb 'despectare' of 396, looking down).

sentences.t:
Infert se saeptus nebula, mirabile dictu,
per medios, miscetque viris, neque cernitur ulli.
sentences.l:
Brings himself, wrapped in mist, marvellous in the telling,
through the midst, and mingles with the men, and is seen by none.
sentences.i: Wrapped in mist—a marvel even to speak of—he walks in among them, mixes with the men, and no one sees him.
sentences.n: 'infert se' — 'carries himself in', 'goes in'. 'saeptus nebula' — 'enclosed in mist' (the perfect participle of 'saepio', as in 'saepsit' of 411; the ablative 'nebula'). 'mirabile dictu' — 'marvellous in the telling': 'dictu' is a supine in -u (ablative of respect, 'in the telling'), a parenthesis. 'per medios' — 'through the midst', the noun ('viros') understood. 'miscet viris' — 'mixes (himself) with the men', the reflexive 'se' understood from 'infert se', with the dative 'viris'. 'neque cernitur ulli' — 'is not seen by anyone': the dative of the agent with a passive verb, which is common in poetry.

sentences.t:
Lucus in urbe fuit media, laetissimus umbra,
quo primum iactati undis et turbine Poeni
effodere loco signum, quod regia Iuno
monstrarat, caput acris equi;
sentences.l:
A grove in the city was in the middle, most luxuriant with shade,
where first, tossed by waves and whirlwind, the Phoenicians
dug up in the place a sign, which royal Juno
had shown, the head of a spirited horse;
sentences.i: In the middle of the city there was a grove, very rich in shade, where the Carthaginians, tossed by waves and storm, first dug up a token that queenly Juno had shown them, the head of a fiery horse;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Lucus in urbe fuit media' — 'a grove in the middle city', the adjective 'media' agreeing with 'urbe', and 'lucus' a sacred wood. 'laetissimus umbra' — 'most rich in shade', with the superlative and the ablative of respect. 'iactati undis et turbine' — 'tossed by waves and storm', the participle echoing Aeneas's own plight (compare 'iactatus' at I.3). 'Poeni' — the Punic people, the Carthaginians (of Phoenician stock; compare 'Poeni' at I.302). 'effodere' — 'effoderunt' ('-ere' for '-erunt'). 'loco' — ablative of place, without 'in'. 'monstrarat' — 'monstraverat', a contracted pluperfect, 'had shown'. 'regia Iuno' — 'queenly Juno'. 'acris equi' — 'of a spirited horse', 'acris' being the genitive singular of 'acer' ('keen, fiery'; do not mistake it for an accusative plural).

sentences.t:
sic nam fore bello
egregiam et facilem victu per saecula gentem.
sentences.l:
for so to be in war
illustrious and easy in living, through the ages, a nation.
sentences.i: for so, she had shown, the people would be, through all ages: renowned in war and easy in their living.
sentences.n: 'sic nam' — 'for thus', with 'nam' put second, not first as it usually is. 'fore' — 'futurum esse', 'would be', in an accusative and infinitive depending on 'monstrarat', 'had shown (that)'. 'gentem' — the subject accusative, held back to the end. 'bello' and 'victu' — ablatives of respect, 'in war', 'in livelihood' ('victus', the fourth-declension noun for 'food, way of life'). The horse's head stands for a people strong in war and prosperous in peace. 'per saecula' — 'through the ages'.

sentences.t:
Hic templum Iunoni ingens Sidonia Dido
condebat, donis opulentum et numine divae,
aerea cui gradibus surgebant limina, nexaeque
aere trabes, foribus cardo stridebat aenis.
sentences.l:
Here a temple to Juno, huge, Sidonian Dido
was founding, rich with gifts and with the godhead of the goddess,
to which of bronze on steps rose the thresholds, and joined
with bronze the beams, on doors the hinge creaked, bronze.
sentences.i: Here Sidonian Dido was building a vast temple to Juno, rich in offerings and in the goddess's power; bronze thresholds rose on its steps, its beams were bound with bronze, and its hinge creaked on doors of bronze.
sentences.n: 'Hic' — 'here', in the grove. 'Sidonia' — 'of Sidon', so 'Phoenician', as 'Tyrian' elsewhere. 'condebat' — imperfect, 'was founding, was building', since the work is not finished. 'donis opulentum et numine divae' — 'rich in gifts and in the godhead of the goddess': the 'numen' is her power, the sense of presence. 'aerea… limina', 'aere trabes', 'foribus… aenis' — three words for bronze in two lines (the adjectives 'aerea' and 'aenis', the noun 'aere'): the temple is a gleam and a clang. 'cui' — 'to which', a dative of reference with 'surgebant', where English says 'whose'. 'nexae' — 'bound together' (perfect participle of 'necto'), agreeing with 'trabes'. 'foribus aenis' — 'on bronze doors', an ablative of place; 'aere' is the ablative of 'aes' ('with bronze'). Juno, who hates the Trojans, is Carthage's patron goddess (I.15–18): the ecphrasis of the Troy paintings that follows takes place in her temple.

sentences.t:
Hoc primum in luco nova res oblata timorem
leniit, hic primum Aeneas sperare salutem
ausus, et adflictis melius confidere rebus.
sentences.l:
This first in the grove a new thing, offered, the fear
eased, here first Aeneas to hope for safety
dared, and for afflicted affairs better to trust.
sentences.i: In this grove a new sight that met him first eased his fear; here Aeneas first dared to hope for safety, and to trust more hopefully in his shattered fortunes.
sentences.n: 'Hoc primum in luco' — 'in this grove first'; the 'hoc' goes with 'luco'. 'nova res oblata' — 'a new thing presented' (perfect participle of 'offero'), the subject of 'leniit'. 'leniit' — 'lenivit', a contracted perfect. 'hic primum' — 'here first': the same 'primum… primum' repeats and marks the turning point. 'ausus' — the perfect participle of the semi-deponent 'audeo', with 'est' understood ('ausus (est)'). 'adflictis… rebus' — 'afflicted affairs' (Greenough's 'adflictis'), the ablative with 'confidere' ('trust in'). 'melius' — 'better', an adverb. 'res' here are his fortunes, a sense that returns at 462.

sentences.t:
Namque sub ingenti lustrat dum singula templo,
reginam opperiens, dum, quae fortuna sit urbi,
artificumque manus inter se operumque laborem
miratur,
sentences.l:
For beneath the huge while he surveys each thing temple,
awaiting the queen, while what the fortune may be to the city,
and of craftsmen the hands among themselves and of works the toil
he marvels at,
sentences.i: For while, under the vast roof, he looks over each thing in turn, waiting for the queen, he marvels at the fortune the city has, at the craftsmen's skill compared hand with hand, and at the toil of their works,
sentences.n: 'namque' — 'for', giving the reason for his heart's rising. 'dum' with the present ('lustrat', 'miratur') — 'while' (an action in progress). 'sub ingenti… templo' — 'beneath the huge temple', the adjective placed first and the noun last. 'singula' — 'each single thing'. 'opperiens' — 'waiting for'. 'quae fortuna sit urbi' — an indirect question with the subjunctive 'sit', 'what fortune there is for the city', 'urbi' a dative of possession: he marvels at the city's luck. 'artificumque manus inter se' — 'the hands of the craftsmen among themselves', i.e. compared with one another, the skill of one against another. 'operum… laborem' — 'the toil of the works'. The first 'dum' has its verb 'lustrat', the second 'miratur'; the cut here is at a comma, and the main verb, 'videt', opens the next unit.

sentences.t:
videt Iliacas ex ordine pugnas,
bellaque iam fama totum volgata per orbem,
Atridas, Priamumque, et saevum ambobus Achillem.
sentences.l:
he sees Trojan in order the battles,
and wars now by fame through the whole spread world,
the Atridae, and Priam, and savage to both Achilles.
sentences.i: he sees the battles of Troy in order, wars already known by report across the whole world, the sons of Atreus, Priam, and Achilles, savage to both sides.
sentences.n: 'videt' — the main verb. 'Iliacas… pugnas' — 'the battles of Ilium', that is Troy; 'ex ordine' — 'in order'. The scene is an ecphrasis (a description of a work of art), as in Homer's Shield of Achilles (Iliad 18). 'volgata' — Greenough's spelling of 'vulgata', 'spread abroad' (perfect participle agreeing with 'bella'). 'fama… per orbem' — 'by report through the world'. 'Atridas' — a Greek accusative plural, 'the sons of Atreus' (Agamemnon and Menelaus). 'saevum ambobus' — 'savage to both': 'ambobus' is a dative of reference, since Achilles raged against Agamemnon in the quarrel of the Iliad and against Priam in killing his son Hector.

sentences.t:
Constitit, et lacrimans, “Quis iam locus inquit Achate,
quae regio in terris nostri non plena laboris?
sentences.l:
He stood still, and weeping, “What now place, says he, Achates,
what region on earth of our not full toil?
sentences.i: He stood still and, weeping, said, “What place is there now, Achates, what region on earth, that is not full of our suffering?
sentences.n: The edition prints the opening speech mark in mid-line, before 'Quis'. 'inquit' is interjected after the first words of the speech, as it normally is, so the line carries its speaker's name in the middle of the question: cut the unit here, at the first question mark. 'Quis iam locus' — 'quis' here is the adjective 'what', 'what place now'. 'Achate' — vocative of 'Achates', his faithful companion ('fidus Achates', I.188). 'nostri… laboris' — 'of our toil': 'nostri' is the possessive adjective agreeing with 'laboris', and the genitive 'laboris' is what 'plena' ('full of') governs. 'regio in terris' — 'region on earth'. Both questions are rhetorical: the Trojan story has reached everywhere.

sentences.t: En Priamus!
sentences.l: Behold, Priam!
sentences.i: Look, there is Priam!
sentences.n: 'En' — 'behold!', pointing to the painting, with a nominative ('Priamus') as the thing pointed to. The sight of the old king (whom Pyrrhus will kill in Book II) stirs him. A short exclamation, cut out as a unit of its own.

sentences.t: Sunt hic etiam sua praemia laudi;
sentences.l: There are here even its own rewards for praise;
sentences.i: Even in this place honour has its own rewards;
sentences.n: 'sunt… praemia' — 'there are rewards'. 'hic' — 'here', at Carthage. 'etiam' — 'even'. 'sua praemia laudi' — 'its own rewards for praise': 'sua' is the possessive, 'laudi' the dative, 'for praise, for glory', that is, for those who earn praise by their deeds. Seeing his own war pictured here, Aeneas takes it that valour is honoured even in this foreign place. The anaphora of 'sunt' links this clause with the next.

sentences.t: sunt lacrimae rerum et mentem mortalia tangunt.
sentences.l: are tears of happenings, and the mind the mortal things touch.
sentences.i: There are tears for what befalls, and the mind is stirred by the lot of mortals.
sentences.n: A set piece listed in conventions.md; the rendering is proposed in new-renderings.md for the owner to confirm. It was built from the Latin alone and kept clear of the familiar English versions. 'sunt lacrimae rerum' — 'there are tears of (for) happenings': 'rerum' is the genitive plural of 'res', and the genitive is deliberately open: tears that belong to events, tears shed for events, tears that events draw out; 'res' in the sense of 'fortunes, circumstances' (as at 452 'adflictis rebus'). 'et mentem mortalia tangunt' — 'mortalia' is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun, 'mortal things, human affairs', the subject; 'mentem' the object, 'the mind'; 'tangunt' 'touch, strike, move'. The two halves are parallel and the line begins with 'sunt', repeating 'sunt' of 461.

sentences.t: Solve metus; feret haec aliquam tibi fama salutem.”
sentences.l: Loose your fears; will bring, this fame, some safety to you.”
sentences.i: Put away your fears; this fame will bring you some measure of safety.”
sentences.n: The end of Aeneas's speech (closing mark after the stop). 'solve metus' — 'loosen your fears' (imperative; 'metus' accusative plural, 4th declension). 'haec… fama' — 'this fame, this renown': the report of Troy's story, which the pictures show has reached even here. 'feret' — future of 'fero'. 'aliquam… salutem' — 'some safety'. 'tibi' — dative of the person benefited.

sentences.t:
Sic ait, atque animum pictura pascit inani,
multa gemens, largoque umectat flumine voltum.
sentences.l:
So he says, and his mind on the empty picture feeds,
much groaning, and with a large stream wets his face.
sentences.i: So he speaks, and feeds his mind on the empty picture, groaning deeply, while a great stream of tears wets his face.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Sic ait' — 'so he speaks'. 'animum pascit' — 'feeds his mind', a metaphor for gazing hungrily. 'pictura… inani' — 'on the empty picture': 'inani' ('empty, unreal') stands after the verb, so that 'pictura… inani' enclose 'pascit'; the picture is only an image. 'multa gemens' — 'groaning much' (the neuter 'multa' as an adverb). 'largo… flumine' — 'with a large stream', i.e. of tears. 'umectat' — 'wets' (Greenough's spelling of 'humectat'). 'voltum' — Greenough's spelling of 'vultum', 'face'.
